newsitem.title: GABON: Gabon election mired in chaos, voters head home.
newsitem.headline: Gabon election mired in chaos, voters head home.

text.p: Gabon's multi-party local elections were beset by chaos on Sunday as many people discovered polling stations were not prepared for voters, witnesses said.
Several hours after polls opened officially at at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT), people headed back home as most polling stations had no ballots, voter lists or even personnel.

Oil-rich Gabon intended the municipal elections as a first test of a 1994 deal between the government and the opposition to set its democratic transition back on course and defuse sometimes bloody political rivalry.
"Out of 10 polling stations in one district of the capital, voting was taking place in only three," said a witness in Libreville.

"Many voters who have been on line at polling stations since six in the morning are heading back home," he said. "There is a heavy security force presence. In some stations soldiers outnumber the voters."
More than 12,000 candidates stood for election as councillors or mayors in the nine provinces of the former Central African French colony.
Politicians complained in the run-up to the poll that voters were showing little enthusiasm for Sunday's ballot.
There was also confusion about the number of people who would be able to vote in the nation of just 1.2 million people.
Voter registration ended on October 17 but election officials said computer generation of 400,000 registration and voting cards was behind schedule.
Commission documents suggested that only 51,213 people had registered to vote in the capital Libreville out of an estimated population of 300,000.

"Many people are leaving town to vote in the country," said Commission logistics commissioner Vincent Mintsa. Candidates were opting to stand in provincial areas with which they had links and supporters were registering outside of Libreville to vote for them, he added.
Under the 1994 Paris accords the municipal elections should have taken place in September 1995.
Legislative elections are now scheduled for November 17, a date criticised by some opposition figures who say it leaves too little time to organise.
President Omar Bongo, vice-president when Gabon gained independence from France in 1960, became head of state in 1968 on the death of Gabon's first president, Leon Mba, and set up a one-party state.
He began moves towards a multi-party system in 1990 after a rash of strikes and demonstrations by students and workers.
Bongo won a five-year term with just over 51 percent of votes cast in a disputed 1993 poll that triggered opposition protests. Five people died in the unrest.

Further clashes followed in 1994, in part to back demands for pay rises after the devaluation that year of the CFA franc used in much of French-speaking Africa. The official death toll was nine, the opposition put the toll at 38.
The Paris Accords between the government and the opposition later that year were designed to increase transparency in government and were approved in a referendum in July 1995.
Legislative elections were planned for early 1996 but delayed. Parliament's mandate ran out in May.
